title: Profile in Resilience: The Marathon of Hope
author: Parker Houston
summary: Houston retells the story of Terry Fox, the young Canadian who, after losing a leg to bone cancer, ran a marathon a day across Canada in his Marathon of Hope to raise cancer research funds before the disease's spread forced him to stop. The piece frames Fox's persistence not as an ability to see the whole 3,339-mile journey in advance, but as a discipline of staying present and focusing only on the day directly in front of him. Houston draws an explicit leadership lesson from this: leaders, parents, and anyone facing an overwhelming future can find relief and clarity by shortening their time horizon to the present moment rather than borrowing tomorrow's troubles. The piece closes with reflection questions inviting the reader to identify a similarly present-focused practice in their own leadership or family life.
points: The central leadership lesson — that Fox's effectiveness came from focusing only on 'the day in front of him' rather than the full scope of an overwhelming goal — offers a concrete reframe for leaders facing long, uncertain projects.

Fox's own words from the cancer ward ('there were brave smiles and those that had given up smiling') are used as direct evidence for why his motivation was other-directed ('my quest would not be a selfish one') rather than personal glory-seeking.

The author explicitly extends the lesson beyond leadership to parenting and personal life, arguing presence-focused thinking is a general antidote to being overwhelmed by scale, not a workplace-specific technique.

The closing quote, 'it took cancer to realize that being self-centered is not the way to live,' is used as the piece's thesis statement connecting personal crisis to a service-oriented leadership philosophy.
quotes: Terry fox didn't know how his story would end. He knew he had cancer and had lost his leg. He knew his cancer could return-but he kept running.
The doctors told him that he would have to have his right leg amputated, followed by 16 months of chemotherapy, and that he had a 50% chance of survival.

There were brave smiles and those that had given up smiling. There were feelings of hopeful denial, and feelings of despair. My quest would not be a selfish one. I could not leave knowing these faces and feelings would still exist, even though I would be set free from mine.
Terry's story illustrates what can happen with a few vital leadership traits-vision, perseverance, courage, living fiercely in the present, and ultimately service and sacrifice for others.
As a leader, a parent, and a human-sometimes I don't know how I will make it through my week, my month, or my year. But in those moments, I need to remember that is not what is being asked of me.
It took cancer to realize that being self-centered is not the way to live. The answer is to try and help others.
